articles.title: Study suggests cognitive skills shape how young children learn new words from screen versus paper books
articles.summary: Reading together on paper or an iPad taught preschoolers new words about equally well on average, new research suggests. Yet how well children comprehended words from a screen hinged on their attention, memory, and self-control skills.

articles.title: Problematic smartphone use predicts a rebound in attention issues during late adolescence
articles.summary: A new study tracking thousands of teenagers found that attention-related symptoms tend to decline in early adolescence before rebounding as adulthood approaches. Researchers discovered that struggling to control smartphone use reliably predicts worse behavioral issues over time.

articles.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
articles.summary: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.summary: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

articles.title: Cynical hostility and lack of assertiveness both predict depression decades later
articles.summary: Tracking 1,017 Swedish twin pairs across 23 years, researchers found that cynical hostility and difficulty saying no both predict worse depression later in life, even between identical twins who share 100 percent of their DNA.

articles.title: Psychologists pooled 80 years of data to answer a basic question about what aging does to our personalities
articles.summary: We know average personalities mature with age, yet psychologists lacked an answer on whether life makes people more alike or pushes them apart. Pooling 362 studies on nearly 400,000 people finally tested that question.

articles.title: Better sexual mentalizing is linked to better sexual function and more sex over time
articles.summary: A four-month study found that the ability to make sense of sexual thoughts and feelings and sexual function predicted each other over time, while sexual satisfaction predicted better sexual mentalizing but not the reverse.

articles.title: Scientists analyzed over 3,700 daily reports to see how personal traits and real-world events relate to your dreams
articles.summary: Using large language models to compare thousands of daily dream and waking reports over four years, researchers mapped how stable personal traits and major real-world events relate to what happens while you sleep.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
articles.summary: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. articles.title: On the loss landscape of the linear neural network: beyond critical points
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.26671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While the critical points of the loss landscape in linear neural networks have been extensively studied since the seminal work of Baldi \& Hornik in the late 1980s, a description of this landscape at an intermediate or global scale is still lacking. Such a characterization is crucial, particularly as a substantial body of literature indicates that gradient descent circumvents critical points. articles.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.26711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output.
